222	
223	Envelope:
224	
225	```json
226	{
227	  "server_id": "uuid",
228	  "epoch": "uuid",
229	  "revision": 1042,
230	  "type": "changed",
231	  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
232	  "at_ms": 1760220000000
233	}
234	```
235	
236	Event types:
237	
238	- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
239	- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
240	- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
241	- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
242	- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
243	- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.
244	
245	**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:
246	
247	1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
248	2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
249	   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
250	   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
251	   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
252	   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
253	   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
254	3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.
255	
256	**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.
257	
258	**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.
259	
260	**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:
261	
262	1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
263	2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
264	3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
265	4. enables commands.
266	
267	Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. 274	- The client's rule per `/ops/{op}` status:
275	  - `done`: use the reply;
276	  - `interrupted`: the host started it and the outcome is unknown; never resubmit; show the session's current state and let the user decide;
277	  - `unknown`: the host never received it (nothing was logged, and the frame answers queued requests in arrival order, so a request that had reached the frame before the status query has a line); resubmitting with the same op is safe.

282	- **A new session (2026-10-19).** `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` opens a session in the project, through the same `session.new` the CLI and Dispatch use, with the body's `op` as the key: `{op, name, kind, cwd, prompt}`, `kind` one of `claude`, `codex` or `shell` (a command or a service is not opened from a device), `cwd` the project's root when absent and otherwise a directory under it, relative or absolute, refused `bad_request` when it steps out of the root or is not a directory, so a device never opens a shell elsewhere on the disk; `prompt` is an agent's first message, on its command line as the CLI puts it, so the agent is already working when the device opens the window. 284	**The draft.** An agent session's prompt on the host is its Prompt Box editor (design.md, "Prompt Box status"), one document with undo, the live utterance as a provisional span, voice commands and the AI pass. A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. The editor exists whether or not the session is drawn on the host, as it does for a card's microphone.

302	## 5. Security and pairing
303	
304	A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
305	
306	- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
307	- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
308	- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
309	- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
310	- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
311	- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
312	- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.

315	- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
316	- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
317	- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
318	- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
319	- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.

321	## 6. Discovery and connection lifecycle
322	
323	### 6.1 Discovery
324	
325	- The host advertises `_switchboard._tcp` while listening on a LAN interface.
326	- The Apple client browses with `Network.framework`.
327	- `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` and `NSBonjourServices` (`_switchboard._tcp`) in the Apple app manifests.
328	- Manual host and port entry for networks where mDNS is blocked.
329	- Known servers and pinned identities are persisted separately from transient discovery results.
330	- A changed IP address is not a new server.
331	- A host that is not connected is resolved again from its Bonjour record before each retry: a host that died sends no goodbye for its old record, so a browse alone does not report the move.
332	- A discovered record whose host is not yet paired offers pairing by the typed code (§5).
333	
334	### 6.2 Per-host state machine
335	
336	`discovered -> unpaired -> pairing -> connecting -> syncing -> connected -> reconnecting/offline`
337	
338	- A failed connection to host A never blocks host B.
339	- Bounded exponential backoff with jitter; reconnect promptly on network changes and on the app returning to the foreground (visionOS and iPadOS drop the socket in the background; cached snapshots cover the gap).
340	- On reconnect: verify the pin, present the token, check `/info` for protocol compatibility and epoch, subscribe, snapshot, reconcile (§4.4), then enable commands.
341	- Errors surface per host.
342	- Unsupported protocol versions are shown explicitly.
343	
344	## 7. Swift client structure
345	
346	Suggested modules:
347	
348	- **SwitchboardProtocol:** Codable models mirroring the wire views, typed requests, version negotiation, the event envelope.
349	- **SwitchboardTransport:** HTTPS/WSS transport with the pinning delegate (`URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` share it), bearer auth, reconnection, discovery.
350	- **SwitchboardClientCore:** `ServerRegistry`, `ConnectionManager`, per-server stores with the event buffer and revision reconciliation, `UnifiedStore`, command routing, cached snapshots with a per-server budget (pages of a conversation evicted furthest from the view first).
351	
352	**What the client keeps, and where.** Persisted, in the app's container: the known-server list (`server_id`, display name, last addresses, enabled flag) and the user's presentation state (workspaces, view instances, window ids, per-view mode and position, server filters). In the Keychain: the bearer token and the pinned key hash per server. **In memory only**: every read model and every content body (session metadata, conversations, last responses, screen text, run output, file content) and any unsent draft. Nothing from a host is written to disk, so there is no data-protection class to choose and no purge schedule; relaunching the client starts from the server list and refetches. Offline, the cached snapshots of §3.2 are what memory holds since the last connection, and they go with the process. Per-server memory budget: 32 MiB of content, evicted furthest from any open view first. **Forget server** removes its token, pin, server entry, memory and every view instance on it; **revocation** or an **identity change** seen on a connection drops the token and the memory at once, marks the server as needing pairing, and keeps the view instances so they can be refilled after a new pairing. A cached body is never shown as current without its connection: every disconnected view says so.
353	- **SwitchboardUI:** shared SwiftUI card, last-response, conversation, run-output, working-set, server selector and connection status views.
354	- **SwitchboardVision:** visionOS entry, spatial `WindowGroup`s, card pop-out lifecycle.
355	- **SwitchboardPad:** iPadOS entry and platform-appropriate multiwindow navigation.
356	
357	One `ServerConnection` actor per known host. The aggregate store exposes qualified references and derived views. UI never builds host URLs to fetch an item.
358	
359	### 7.1 Presentation model
360	
361	Separate:
362	
363	1. **Resource:** a session, working set or pinned file owned by a server.
364	2. **View instance:** a presentation of that resource, with mode (`compact`, `last_response`, `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output`), selection, scroll and disclosure state, and a unique view-instance id. The mode set depends on the session's kind: `conversation` and `last_response` exist for Claude Code sessions, `screen` for every running session, `run_output` for commands and services.
365	3. **Workspace:** a saved collection of view instances and client-side organization. **A workspace is cross-host by construction**: its view instances refer to qualified resources, so one workspace may hold views on any combination of paired servers, with no coordinating server and no host-side resource for it. A host's working sets stay host-owned (§8); a workspace is the client's own grouping over them.
366	
367	The same resource can be shown in several views without duplicating anything. Client-side window and view state is never sent to the host. The per-server store counts the view instances interested in each content key and sends `watch` and `unwatch` only on the transitions between zero and one (§4.4).
368	
369	### 7.2 visionOS windows
370	
371	- Main window: combined browsing with list, grid and focus modes and server filters. Card sizes follow the host's grid rectangles only as a hint; the client lays out for its own space.
372	- Card window group: `WindowGroup(for: CardWindowRequest.self)` keyed by a stable window-instance id and a qualified ref.
373	- `openWindow` and `dismissWindow` create and close windows; the system positions them.
374	- Closing a window never stops a session.
375	- Per-view mode and navigation state survive, keyed by `(resume_id, turn n)` for conversation position.
376	- When a server goes offline, windows stay open on cached content with controls disabled. A `removed` event marks the window and disables its controls; the window stays until the user closes it.
377	
378	### 7.3 iPadOS reuse
379	
380	- Reuse protocol, transport, stores, presentation models and most views.
381	- Adapt multiwindow behavior to iPadOS scenes.
382	- No RealityKit or visionOS-only APIs in shared packages.
383	
384	## 8. Unified browsing and filtering
385	
386	- Default view: all connected hosts, with source labels.
387	- Filter by server, working set, session kind, and state (`CardState` labels: waiting on you, working, idle, starting, exited, not running, not resumable).
388	- Sorting across hosts: the host's own rank (waiting first, then working, starting, idle, exited, not running, mirroring `CardState::rank`), then last activity, then record id as the tie-breaker.
389	- Server management screen: discovered and known servers, status, pairing, rename, enable/disable, forget.
390	- Working sets with the same name on different servers stay separate by qualified id; the UI groups by source.
391	- No client-made cross-host working set in v1. The host's sets are read-only from the client.
392	
393	## 9. Remote access later
394	
395	Every server is an authenticated endpoint; nothing assumes RFC1918 addresses or Bonjour. A future Tailscale or WireGuard route, a manual remote endpoint, or an outbound relay reuses the same protocol, token and pinned key. No relay in v1. The pin is bound to the installation's key, not to an address or a certificate's validity window, so a route change or a reissued certificate does not invalidate it.
396

### Trust boundary

Switchboard executes commands from records, so where records come from
matters. A record that arrived via `git clone` or a branch checkout must
never run anything on its own.

- **Milestone 1: private state only.** Records live under Application
  Support and are written only by Switchboard on this machine. Nothing in
  a project directory is executed or even parsed as configuration.
- **Shareable config (built 2026-09-08).** A committed
  `<root>/.switchboard/project.json` carries command and service
  definitions with the variable names they expect (never values). It
  never carries transcripts, secrets, or live-session state. Its contents
  are shown, not run, until the user approves each entry; approval
  records a hash of the entry on the record, and any change or new entry
  requires approval again. Autostart from shared config is never honored
  without that approval. The file is capped at 64 KiB and refused when
  it is a symlink; the README documents its schema.
- **Secrets** come from the Keychain and from `.env` files the user
  already owns; Switchboard writes them nowhere else. They leave the app
  only as `new-session -e` written to the tmux client's stdin
  (`start-server ; source-file -`, spike 18), or as the `env.resolve`
  reply on the owner-only `control.sock` to `switchboard-env`, which
  puts them in its child's environment and nowhere else. Neither is a
  command line, so no value reaches the client's argv or the server's,
  which keeps the argv of the client that started it. `env.resolve`
  answers only the holder of a record's launch token
  (`SWITCHBOARD_RECORD_TOKEN`, new at every spawn, its SHA-256 on the
  record), so a session resolves only its own grants; the token is as
  private as the pane's environment. The same token gates
  `session.ask`, which marks only its holder's own record as asking the
  owner something. The one other way a secret's surroundings leave the
  app is as redacted text on the remote port: a paired device reads a
  pane's screen with every value Switchboard holds for the project
  replaced by its name, and the port's key and tokens never reach a
  record or a log.
  The writes (`env.set.upsert`, `env.secret.store`, `env.grant`) are
  accepted only inside a five-minute setup window the owner opens from
  the app's settings menu, so an agent cannot grant itself a set. What a
  child prints reaches the agent's tool result and the provider's
  transcript: the owner accepts that by granting a set. Scrollback can
  contain secrets that a process printed; it is stored privately, capped,
  rotatable, and deletable, and the UI says so. Agent transcripts stay
  where the provider keeps them; Switchboard reads them and never edits
  one. The one write is cloning a session, which puts a *new* transcript
  (a prefix of the original under a fresh id, owner-readable only)
  beside the original; spike 7 has the mechanism.

  a change page after page to the end; a turn over 256 KiB loses its tool detail and
  notes first, then its prompt is shortened, then its answer is cut
  from the front, and says `truncated`), `session.last_response` (the
  last turn's answer, a projection of the conversation key at its
  revision), `session.runs` (from the record, artifacts by name) and
  `session.run_output` (the log's tail, 500 lines at most). The
  content worker reads them all: a transcript is parsed through the
  reader's new `read_masked`, which runs the mask over every text
  before the parser's caps, and the parsed, masked conversation stays
  on the worker by handle, file version and policy, so a poll is a
  stat and a page is served from memory; a run's log is read through
  `scrollback::tail_masked`, which starts the longest secret's length
  before the tail window so a value on the window's edge is masked
  whole, and is versioned by inode, change time and size. The key for
  a run is `record/n`, and the diff pass fingerprints a record's runs
  as the `runs` collection. Only a Claude Code session has a
  conversation; the rest are refused `no_conversation`. The client
  holds a conversation as pages merged by turn number (`ConversationState`):
  a `changed {conversation}` refetches from the last turn held, which
  replaces that turn and everything after, a page reaching the end
  drops anything after it, and another `resume_id` drops it all; the
  card windows draw Last response (the answer with its inline
  Markdown), Conversation (each turn's prompt, its activity folded
  under a line with the tool calls' input and result one level deeper,
  its answer; "Earlier turns" loads the page ending before the first held;
  the end follows the host) and Run output (a run picker with its
  status and the tail, scaled like the screen). Seen on the simulator
  against a throwaway host: a real transcript's last page scrolled to
  its end, and a service's run with its exit code and log. Not yet in
  C: `file.read` (no view asks for a file before Milestone D) and the
  policy reads off the frame.
- **C3, the control scope.** `POST sessions/{id}/send|resume|trust`
  for a device whose scope is `control` (a read device is refused
  `scope`, by name, with nothing run). The body carries the device's
  own operation id, `op`, and for a send the text (16 KiB at most).
  The request becomes the wire request the control socket would carry
  and goes through the same `serve`, so nothing new runs or logs: a
  send or a resume is written to `operations.log` before it runs, a
  repeat of the op is answered from the log without typing or
  launching again, and an op that was started and never answered is
  refused `interrupted` (409) rather than run twice. `/info` lists
  `control` among the capabilities and the send and op caps among the
  limits. The client makes a UUID per command and follows the spec's
  rule on a timeout: a status query, never a blind resend; `done`
  takes the logged reply (its failure reason included), `interrupted`
  is shown as started with the outcome unknown, `unknown` resends once
  with the same op. A `scope` refusal names the reason and keeps the
  pairing (only an unauthorized or revoked token drops it), and a
  timeout on a command does not count against the connection. The
  card window of a Claude session ends in a control bar: a message
  field with a microphone button that starts dictation at once
  through the Speech framework, on-device where the device has it,
  the words revised in place after what was typed (the keyboard's own
  mic still works; "look to dictate" is a system affordance of search
  fields only, and an app gets no gaze event, so the button is a tap),
  Send, "Trust this folder" when the session view
  carries the question, and Resume for a not-running session with a
  handle, behind "Resume spends a turn". The bar is disabled unless
  the session is live, and a read device sees why instead of the
  controls. Tests cover a read device refused, a send typed once for
  one op, a resume launching once, a running one launching nothing,
  trust answering the question once, the bad bodies, and the scope
  lowered again; on the client the op per command, the three status
  outcomes after a timeout, the one resend and the give-up, and the
  refusals.
- **C3, the draft.** An agent session's prompt as a device reads and
  works on it is its Prompt Box editor on the host, made on demand as
  the card's microphone makes one (`prompt_box::ensure_editor`).
  `GET sessions/{id}/draft` answers the editor's rendered text, the
  live utterance's range, its status and what undo, redo and the AI
  pass can do (`DraftView`); `POST` with `action` applies replace,
  undo, redo, clear, clean_up, delete_sentence or delete_paragraph,
  or `send` with the device's `op`, which takes the draft to the pane
  through `serve` as the plain send does and clears the editor (a
  repeat of a send that went is answered from the log; an empty draft
  is refused); `POST sessions/{id}/dictation` feeds a device's speech
  events (`started`, `voice_started`, `partial`, `final`,
  `voice_ended`, `stopped`, with the device's own recognizer session
  number) to the editor as `SpeechEventReceived`, so the device
  recognizes and the editor keeps the document. The drafts are
  fingerprinted every 150 ms while a subscriber is connected and an
  editor that moved emits `changed {draft, id}`; the device holding it
  re-reads. `/info` lists the `draft` capability. The client's
  control bar on such a host is a view of the editor: typing replaces
  the text once it pauses, dictation goes as speech events in order
  with a recognizer session per run, the tools sit above the field,
  Send goes through the draft under an op, and `changed {draft}`
  re-reads what a bar holds. The prompt window on the headset
  (`PromptWindowView`, one per app) shows the whole draft of the
  session whose input is active, the live utterance in amber, with a
  microphone, the tools and Send, the desktop preview's role for the
  Working Set. Known gaps: the AI
  pass runs in the editor's worker, pumped by the host's frame, so a
  host whose window is occluded finishes it on its next frame; the
  Mac's own voice runtime and a device dictate into the same editor
  under different session numbers, and nothing stops both at once.
- **C3, restoration.** A card window keeps its place in a
  conversation (`ConversationPlace`): the turn at the top of the view,
  or the end it follows, and the folds open per turn and per activity,
  keyed by the transcript's `resume_id`. The scroll view is positioned
  by turn number, so a page merging under the view keeps the turn at
  the top where it is, and "Earlier turns" pins the turn that was
  first; the end is followed only while the end marker is on screen,
  so reading an old turn while the agent works no longer jumps. The
  folds live in the window rather than the rows, so a turn replaced by
  a refetch, or the whole conversation dropped and re-read on a
  reconnect, comes back with the same folds open. The place is saved
  beside the window's mode in `presentation.json` (an older file reads
  with no place), so a relaunch restores it; a turn no longer held
  after a reconnect, or another transcript, falls back to the end.
- **C4, the policy off the frame and `file.read`.** The frame no
  longer resolves a redaction policy: a content job carries a
  `PolicySpec` (the project's environment, the sets it and the session
  may use, and `policy_epoch`, moved by every save and secret change)
  and the content worker reads the dotenv files and the secret store,
  caching the policy per spec for a minute, so a slow Keychain call
  costs the worker, never a frame; `Services.secrets` is an `Arc` for
  that. A store that fails refuses with `policy` (503) rather than
  answering unmasked. `GET projects/{id}/files/{path}` reads a file
  some working set pins (`PinTarget::File`), through
  `adapters::files::open_pinned`: the path checked before the disk,
  the root opened as a directory descriptor and every component
  opened from the previous one with `NOFOLLOW` (no symlink is followed,
  parent or leaf; macOS says `ENOTDIR` where Linux says `ELOOP`), the
  leaf non-blocking so a FIFO does not park the thread and checked to
  be a regular file, dotenv names refused whatever is pinned, the read
  one byte past the 768 KiB limit so growth cannot pass it, the version
  the inode, change time and size. The worker caches the masked file
  per key and re-reads only when the version or the policy moved; a
  watched file emits `changed {file, project/path}` on the poll.
  Refusals: `not_pinned` (404), `too_large` (413, with the size),
  `failed` (400) for a dotenv file, a symlink, a FIFO or a non-text
  file. The client holds files as content (`FileBody`, `watch(file:)`,
  re-read on `changed`); no window shows one yet, which the working set
  view brings. Milestone C is complete.
- **Scope on the listings.** A listing over the remote port leaves
  out the records Dispatch made for its own use (a ticket's project
  and its sessions, a worker session anywhere), told by the
  `<ticket>-<nonce>` op they were made under
  (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`); a supervisor's
  (`sup-…`) and the owner's own stay. `?scope=all` on `projects`,
  `sessions`, `waiting` and the `events` subscription lists and
  announces them, and a worker record is still read by its id, for
  the ticket view to come. Frames for a worker record go to `scope=all`
  subscribers alone. The control socket is untouched, so Dispatch sees
  everything as before.
- **On the headset (2026-10-14).** Scene restoration is ruled out: a
  launch opens the Sessions window and nothing else (the card and
  prompt window groups have `restorationBehavior(.disabled)`), after a
  restored window kept the process alive out of view so that an icon
  tap presented nothing. A launch log in the app's container
  (`launch.log`: launches, window appearances, scene phases) stands in
  for a device syslog the Mac cannot read. The conversation's end
  marker lives outside the lazy stack, so the follow button and
  opening at the end hold on the device. Following the end was then
  made a mode (2026-10-16): the view is held at the end with scrolling
  off, and anything growing under it pulls the end back on screen; a
  button at the right edge releases it to read, the ellipsis at the
  foot returns it. Before, following meant "the marker is on screen",
  and a new turn's row growing after the scroll landed pushed the
  marker off and turned following off by itself; the turn at the top
  was also a position bound to the scroll view, which re-applied it as
  the content grew and sent the view up. Markdown tables in an answer
  are laid out as grids. A Bonjour resolve that gets no answer is
  given up after 5 s, and each offline host resolves on its own task,
  after the retry loop hung on one resolve left waiting by the system.
- **Tickets on the headset (2026-10-17).** The port serves Dispatch's
  tickets from the app's own status poll (`src/core/tickets.rs`, spec
  §4.7): a listing by project with each ticket's standing worded as the
  Mac's page words it and its decisions; one ticket with its body,

  when Dispatch answers the call the Mac's action became

  tickets are one fingerprinted collection, so a device hears one
  `changed tickets` frame per status that moved. The client lists them
  on a Tickets tab, oldest first within a project, urgent ones marked,
  with a detail view that answers decisions (the recommended option
  first, a note field, several options for a `multiple` one), resumes
  a parked ticket, and opens the project's supervisor session.
  The next day (2026-10-18) the attempts' files came: each attempt
  lists its artifacts, checks log, review rounds' files and evidence
  by a key that stands for the path, the port reads one as text
  through the Mac's own artifact read (from its cache while the ticket
  stands) or as an image from the disk, serves the ticket's events
  from the Mac's cache, and takes `close`; `info` lists `evidence` for
  it. The client's list is ordered last-moved-first with a menu for
  the order (waiting first, newest, by project), the hosts, projects
  and states (closed hidden unless asked), and a "waiting on me"
  switch; the detail shows each attempt's checks and rounds with a
  button per readable file, a Notes shortcut to the newest notes, a
  timeline, and Close. Left out for now: take, the console, the plan
  review's feedback flow; a worker session is named but not opened,
  since the plain listing hides worker records.
- **A session opened from the headset (2026-10-19).** The port takes
  `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` (spec §4.5): the
  body's `op` the key, through the control socket's `session.new`,
  a Claude Code, Codex or shell session named by the device, in the
  project's root or a directory under it (`project_dir` in `app.rs`
  refuses a path that steps out or is not a directory), an agent's
  `prompt` its first turn on the command line. `info` lists `create`,
  and `/ops/{op}` names what a done creation made, so a lost reply
  still finds its record. The client offers a plus button on the
  Sessions tab and "New session in this project" on a listed session
  for a host that is connected, paired under `control` and serves
  `create`; the sheet (`NewSessionView.swift`) picks the host, the
  project by workspace, the kind, a name (defaulting to the kind's
  word and a count), a directory and the first message, and Start
  opens the session's window on the reply. Not from a device yet:
  commands and services, environment sets on the new session, a new
  project or workspace.
- **Pairing by the typed code (2026-10-14).** visionOS gives an app
  no camera, so the QR code is never scanned on the headset. A
  discovered host that is not paired offers Pair on the Servers screen:
  the client resolves its record, reads `/info` under no trust and
  shows the key the host presented in the dialog's own short form
  (`KeyFingerprint.short`, the first sixteen hex digits in fours), the
  owner compares it with the Key line on the Mac and types the
  eight-character code, and the pairing goes out pinned to that key
  (`ConnectionManager.lookup` and `pair(_:code:)`; the resolver is
  injectable for the tests). Pasting the invite's text stays as the
  fallback.
- **Known gaps at the first merge.** Milestone D, the iPad shell, is
  not started. The Codex transcript parser, so a Codex session's
  conversation is empty on a device. The Dispatch ticket view
  (`scope=all` is served; no view asks for it). Removing dead sessions

  screen and run-output modes follow the end without the

523	
524	## 13. Explicit design decisions
525	
526	| Decision | v1 choice |
527	|---|---|
528	| Topology | Independent hosts, no coordinator |
529	| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
530	| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
531	| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
532	| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
533	| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
534	| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
535	| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
536	| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
537	| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
538	| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
539	| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
540	| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
541	| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
542	| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
543	| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
544	| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
545	| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
546	| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
547	| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
548	| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
549	| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
550	| Presentation state | Client-owned |
551	| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |
552	| Remote internet access | Deferred; protocol-compatible |
553	| iPadOS | Shared Swift core and views |

## 10. Delivery plan and acceptance criteria

### Spike 22 — `spikes/22-remote-port`

Before any host code, with measured results in its README:

- A blocking HTTPS server over `std::net::TcpListener` with `rustls` and an `rcgen` certificate, a WebSocket upgrade with `tungstenite`, and requests handed to a stand-in "frame" thread over a bounded `mpsc`, as the control socket does. Measure request latency through the handoff at the app's frame rate while hidden.
- **Frame cost, measured, with targets.** The frame's share of a metadata request, a content handle lookup, a worker's version action and the read-model diff over a few hundred records, each timed per pass; the target is under 1 ms per pass for the port's whole share, and under 4 ms at the 99th percentile with 8 requests in a pass. The content work on the connection thread timed separately: the largest transcript in the user's data directory parsed and masked (its time and peak memory are the supported size for §4.3), a 768 KiB file read and masked, a Keychain read made slow (a locked keychain) and shown to stall only its connection. A stalled subscriber and 20 connections that stall after the TLS handshake, with a healthy paired client and the frame loop measured through both. The README records the numbers and the thresholds, and a pass that misses the target is a design finding, not a tuning note.
- **Content versions.** The signals of §4.4 against the cases that defeat weaker ones: a same-size in-place rewrite of a pinned file with mtime restored by `touch -r`, a replace-by-rename, a run log truncated and regrown to the same length, a transcript appended within one poll interval; each must move the version. The two-second `stat` poll over 128 keys timed.
- Bonjour advertisement from the Rust process on macOS, visible to a visionOS simulator; the crate or system path that works.
- `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` on visionOS accepting the self-signed certificate through a pinning delegate that checks the SPKI hash and nothing weaker; the same delegate refusing a substituted certificate.
- The `openat` walk of §4.3 through `rustix` or `cap-std`: a pinned FIFO with no writer refused at once on its connection thread while the frame loop and a second connection keep going; a parent directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk refused.
- Two instances on one machine (`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR`, `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=switchboard-test-*`, different ports) each advertising with its own key.

Loopback-only and no auth are fine here and nowhere else.

**Results (2026-10-12, `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`).** The host
half ran: the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass against the 1 ms
target; a request's latency is one frame interval, since a client that
sends on the reply synchronizes with the frame; the pools, the 5 s
handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
20 stalled connections and an unread socket, with a paired client
unaffected; a wrong pin fails at the handshake; `mdns-sd` advertises
and `dns-sd` sees it; the 146 MB largest transcript parses in 290 ms at
575 MB peak, which is why content work is off the frame; ctime and
inode catch the same-size rewrite, the rename and the regrown log. Two
amendments follow: content reads go to **one worker thread** with a
queue rather than each connection thread, so one large parse is in
memory at a time (§4.1 is read with that change), and the Bonjour
instance name carries a short id suffix beside the display name. Not
run: the visionOS pinning delegate and the read-model diff timing.

### Milestone A — Host port and multi-host client foundation

Five commits, each leaving the app running and each with its README and design.md status update. The first user-visible result is a two-host read-only client at A2; nothing waits for the synchronization machinery.

**A0 — The conversation cache in the app.** `UiState.conversations` moves to `SwitchboardApp` as the first content cache, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version; the session, card and workflow views read it through a reference. No port code. Acceptance: the UI tests pass unchanged and the app behaves identically.

**A1 — Identity and an authenticated read-only host.** `identity.json` (id, certificate, `server_name` and the listen preference: off the LAN by default, loopback until enabled), the key in the Keychain under its installation's account, `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. `ports::remote`, `adapters/remote.rs` with the bounds of §4.1 and the two-step content handoff, a fake, the `Effect` and `AppAction` arms, the allowlist, the redaction function. The pairing window and QR code in the settings menu, the paired-devices dialog with scope and Revoke, `devices.json`. Endpoints: `/info`, `/pair`, projects, spaces, sets, one set, sessions, session, waiting, screen. No events yet; a reply carries `epoch` and `revision` from the counter, which only the diff of A3 will move. The screen is answered on the frame as the control port answers it (a pane snapshot, redacted); the worker handoff arrives with the screen cache of A4, since there is nothing to version before it. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status.* Tests: `tests/remote.rs` against a real socket with fakes, modelled on `tests/control.rs`, covering pairing, the pin check, scope, revocation, the allowlist and screen redaction; a UI test for the dialog. Acceptance: a paired `curl` with the pinned certificate reads every view over the LAN; an unpaired one gets `/info` and nothing else.

**A2 — Two hosts and the first client.** Bonjour advertisement and the Linux stub. The Swift protocol, transport with the pinning delegate, `ServerRegistry`, `ConnectionManager`, and a read-only browser of sessions and sets with source labels, refreshing on a timer. *Built 2026-10-12 as the package under `client/` with a command-line browser for the Mac; the app targets come with Milestone B; see design.md's remote client status.* Acceptance: two installations have distinct `server_id`s and keys; Bonjour discovers both; the client pairs with both and connects simultaneously; nothing mixes identifiers; taking one offline leaves the other working and its items visibly stale; a changed IP reconnects under the same pin.

**A3 — Synchronization.** The read-model diff after every pass, the revision counter moving, `changed` and `removed` events for metadata and collections, the WebSocket with `hello`, subscribe-then-snapshot and reconciliation by revision on the client, epoch handling, `resync_required`. `ops` and the log-before-run path in `serve` (no commands yet, but the path is tested here). *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. A global collection's `id` is the empty string; the diff runs only on passes that dispatched something; the `runs` collection waits for its endpoint.* Acceptance: the timer refresh of A2 is gone and every host-side change reaches the client within a pass; the mutation-between-hello-and-snapshot test passes on both sides.

**A4 — Watched content.** The watch set and its worker poll, `watch` and `unwatch` with `watching`, content versions for screen (the other content kinds arrive with Milestone C and use the same cache), eviction, the policy fingerprint in the cache key, the overflow close. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. The worker reads a pane's whole window so a short read and the poll see one version; the policy is resolved and cached on the frame (cleared by any save or secret change) until Milestone C moves the secret reads off it; a key held only by a subscriber has no read time and goes with its last `unwatch`.* Acceptance: a watched pane's screen updates live while the host shows an unrelated view or is hidden; the abuse tests of §4.1 pass against the real adapter.

Across A1 to A4: README (Layout, dev aids, data directory) and the design.md status section, with the trust boundary's sentence on redacted text added at A1.

### Milestone B — Native visionOS browser

- Grid, list and focus browsing of real sessions and sets from two hosts.
- Two items from different servers open as independent spatial windows.
- Each window offers `compact` and `screen`; the other modes arrive with Milestone C and the window says so until then.
- Closing a window never ends a session.
- Reconnect preserves open windows and refreshes them through subscribe-then-snapshot.

*Built 2026-10-12 on the visionOS simulator, three commits (B1 the app shell on an xcodegen project, B2 card windows, B3 browsing and persistence); see design.md's remote client status. The headset itself waits on the one-time Xcode device setup.*

### Milestone C — Interactive sessions

- `session.conversation`, `session.last_response`, `session.runs`, `session.run_output` and `file.read` on the wire and the port, with `read_pinned` in the files adapter, `read_masked` on the transcript reader and the overlap read in `scrollback`.
- Conversation paging by turn, with the body cap, the oversized turn, the in-progress last turn and the rebind handled.
- `send`, `resume` and `trust` under `control` scope, with the operation id as the idempotency key and `/ops/{op}` on timeout.
- Live updates over the WebSocket through the watch set; scroll and disclosure restoration across incremental refetches and reconnects.
- System dictation into the text field as the initial voice input.

*C1 and C2 built 2026-10-13 (the content endpoints but `file.read`, the conversation paged and merged, the three modes drawn), C3 the same day (`send`, `resume` and `trust` under the control scope through the control socket's `serve` and log, the op the key, `/ops/{op}` on a timeout; a control bar on a Claude session's window with a microphone button that dictates through the Speech framework; the conversation view's place, scroll and folds, kept across merges, reconnects and relaunches); see design.md's remote client status. `file.read` and the policy reads off the frame remain. C4 the same day: `file.read` (`GET projects/{id}/files/{path}`, a file some working set pins, read through the descriptor walk of §4.3 in `adapters::files::open_pinned` on the content worker, versioned by inode, change time and size, masked, refused `not_pinned`, `too_large` with its size, or `failed` for a dotenv file, a symlink or a non-text file) and the policy resolved on the worker: the frame hands the worker what names a policy (`PolicySpec`: the project environment, the sets, an epoch moved by every save and secret change) and the worker reads the dotenv files and the secret store, caching per spec, so a slow Keychain call never costs a frame. Milestone C is complete.*

### Milestone D — Shared iPadOS shell

- The same modules and components on iPad with platform-appropriate navigation and windows.

*Not started; Milestones A to C merged without it (2026-10-14).*

## 11. Tests and failure cases

Host, in `tests/remote.rs` and the adapter's own tests unless said otherwise:

- Two hosts produce the same `RecordId` (seeded in fakes): no collision in UI or routing (client).
- A host's IP changes; Bonjour rediscovers it under the same pinned key (client, spike).
- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).
- A substituted certificate during first pairing: the client refuses to send the code; and a `/pair` carrying another host's `spki_sha256` is refused by the host.
- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. Twenty unauthenticated connections and a `/pair` flood past the per-minute cap: a paired client's requests are answered throughout, the flood gets 429 and closed sockets.
- After Revoke, the device's next request fails and its WebSocket is closed. After a key rotation, `devices.json` is empty, every old token fails, and the dialog says the pairings are gone; the client, seeing the new key under a known `server_id`, sends nothing and asks to pair again.
- A scope lowered in the dialog refuses the device's next `send`; raised, allows it; no request over the port changes a scope.
- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. A failed request-line append refuses the send and sends nothing. A dropped HTTP response after a logged reply is answered from the log.
- `unknown` for an op that never reached the frame; a resubmit runs once.
- The configured secret appears in a prompt, a tool result, a final response, a run's output, and a pinned non-dotenv text file: every content endpoint returns it masked. A secret store that fails makes every content endpoint refuse rather than answer.
- The configured secret straddles each cut: the parser's `DETAIL_CAP` inside a tool result, the 256 KiB turn cut, the first byte of a run-output tail window, and the front cut of a last response: each reply masks it whole or drops it whole, never a fragment.
- A project with three hundred sessions, each with 64 KiB notes and a 100 KiB `name`, listed whole: one reply under the cap, notes cut at 4 KiB and names at 4 KiB with each field in `truncated`, no member lost; the same session read alone carries its notes whole. A session entering and leaving `waiting` emits `changed {waiting}` and the refetched collection lacks or holds it accordingly; a member missing from a whole reply at a later revision is dropped by the client, a member missing from an older reply arriving late is not.
- A 700 KiB file of quotation marks is under the source limit and answers `too_large` from the serialized check; a pane with 200 lines of 4 KiB each is cut by bytes after masking and marked. A pinned file over the source limit answers `too_large`; a last response over the body cap is cut from the front and marked.
- Content versions (F2): a pinned file rewritten in place at the same size with its mtime restored, a file replaced by rename, a run log truncated and regrown to its old length, and a transcript appended twice within one poll interval: each read after the change carries new content and a new revision, and no two different bodies for one key share a revision within an epoch. Two reads of an unchanged file carry the same revision.
- Frame cost (F4): a 20 MiB transcript, a 768 KiB file and a Keychain read made to block for two seconds, each requested while a second connection reads session metadata: the metadata reply arrives within a pass and the frame's time per pass stays under its budget; only the requesting connection waits. A content handle read on the frame for a record removed before the worker finishes: the worker's version action is a no-op and the reply names the handle it read.
- A window on the last response alone, and one on the conversation, each refresh when the transcript grows with no session metadata change; a handle rebind refreshes both.
- With every content cache populated, a new environment-set grant, a changed secret value, and a secret store that starts failing: unchanged screen, file and run-output sources are not served from their old masked bytes; the first two emit `changed` for the watched keys and serve newly masked text, the third refuses.
- A watched session's transcript grows and a watched pinned file is edited while the host shows an unrelated project, a document, the Dispatch page, and while the window is hidden: `changed` arrives within the poll interval.
- A space rename, a session moved between projects, a project and a session removed, a time-based rule set losing a member: the right `changed` and `removed` events, no reconnect.
- A set renamed and a pin moved (saved through `SaveViews`), a Claude Code pane reaching its trust question (`PromptSeen`, no save), and a Codex pane passing its quiet interval (`HostListed`, no save, no screen change): each emits `changed` for the right resource within the pass. - Two reads of a watched file, a transcript and a pane separated by an external edit with no poll between them, delivered to the client in reverse order: the client ends on the newer content. A read of a session's metadata between them does not invalidate the conversation page.
- Closing one of two windows on a session sends no `unwatch`; closing the second does. A hundred and twenty-nine watched keys against the cap of 128: the least recently read is evicted, a read of it still answers with the right version and re-enters it, and no watch is refused. Reconnect resends the watches before any snapshot.

- The subscriber queue overflows: `resync_required`, the socket closes, the host's frame loop and a second subscriber are unaffected (spike and adapter test).
- 20 stalled unauthenticated connections: the port stays answerable to a paired client (spike).

- A long transcript pages by turn; one enormous turn is cut and marked; a conversation whose handle changed answers with the new `resume_id` and the client refetches from 1 (client).
- An exited command whose pane is gone: `screen` refuses, `runs` and `run_output` answer from the log; a pruned log answers with the reason.

# Notes for issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port

Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/design.md (Trust boundary, Remote client 2026-10-12 and its status entries), docs/lessons.md, docs/remote-client.md in full. Line numbers below are from this worktree (branch `dispatch/230-...`, at "Release 0.4.1"). Nothing was run: no build, no test, no browser.

## 1. On-disk record and rehydration (before any pane)

Workspaces are data, processes are a cache. The web surface adds almost no new durable data, and the notes say where the tree currently has none.

- **Already durable, and enough for a browser device.** `devices.json` (`PairedDevice` in `src/ports/remote.rs`: id, name, scope, `token_sha256`, created, last_seen) and `identity.json` (`Identity`: server_id, name, certificate, `spki_sha256`, listen). A browser is one more `PairedDevice`. Revocation is `AppAction::RevokeDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86`) deleting the row. That is the whole server-side record. No schema bump is needed unless a field is added to `PairedDevice` (e.g. a device "kind" or user-agent string). `#[serde(default)]` would make that additive, but `identity.json`/`devices.json` have their own versioning (`IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION`), not `SCHEMA_VERSION`. [tree] to confirm whether a `devices.json` change needs a migration step.
- **No tombstone for a revoked device.** A revoked token and a never-known token are the same thing to the host: `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`) answers 401 `unauthorized`, "the token is not known; pair again". The acceptance line "revoke the phone and the page says so on its next request" cannot be met from the current reply. It would need either a tombstone (hash of revoked tokens, a new durable record) or the page saying "not paired or revoked" for both. The issue asks for "revoked" and "identity changed" to be said plainly, so this is a decision.
- **The page's own state (client side), rehydrated per load:** the token (a cookie or `localStorage`, decision 2), the pinned `spki_sha256` and `server_id` from the pairing URL, the last revision. Everything else (sessions, conversation, screen) is in memory and refetched, as the Swift client does (§7 "What the client keeps": nothing from a host on disk). Rehydration of a page = load HTML, read the stored credential, `GET /api/v1/info`, open `/api/v1/events`, wait for `hello`, fetch snapshots, apply buffered events by revision (§4.4 "Subscribe first, then snapshot"). The existing protocol already gives that; the page re-implements the Swift client's reconcile (per-key held revision, epoch change refetches everything, `resync_required` reconnects).
- **The pairing window** is not saved (`PairingWindow` in core, `OpenPairing` at `src/core/remote.rs:46`; code made by `remote::pairing_code()`, 40 bits, single use, three failures close it). A URL carrying the code is therefore valid only while that in-memory window is open.
- **Host-side secrets:** key in Keychain as `remote-key:<server_id>`; token never stored, only its SHA-256. A web token in a cookie does not change this, but "keep tokens out of logs, URLs" (§5 line 318) now meets a request line that contains the code (see 3.4).

## 2. What exists, with files and lines

### The port (adapter): `src/adapters/remote.rs`
- `RemoteRequest` `:360` carries method, path (query stripped), query pairs, body, `bearer`, `upgrade`. There is **no cookie, no Origin, no Host, no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, no User-Agent field**. Only `authorization`, `upgrade`, `sec-websocket-key`, `content-length` are read in `read_request` (`:444`, bearer at `:487`, upgrade at `:491`); every other header is dropped. The user-agent for a device name (issue item 6) would be a new field.
- `RemoteReply` `:389` is `{status, body, authenticated}`: **no content type, no extra headers**. `respond` (`:530`) hardcodes `Content-Type: application/json` and `Connection: keep-alive`, with a status table that has no 304 and no 308. There is no `Set-Cookie`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `Cache-Control` or `X-Content-Type-Options` anywhere (grep found none). `RemoteReply { .. }` is built by struct literal in about 28 places in `src/app.rs` (count from grep) plus the adapter, so adding a field is a mechanical but wide edit, unless a constructor or `Default` is added first.
- `respond_upgrade` (`:519`) writes a 101 with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered a subprotocol and gets none back fails the connection (see Open questions), so the subprotocol candidate needs a change here as well as in `read_request`.
- `connection` (`:770`): TLS handshake with 5 s (`HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT :570`), then a request/reply loop; first request within 5 s then `IDLE_TIMEOUT` 30 s (`:573`). `Limits::limited` (`:631`) rate-limits **only** `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and `/api/v1/info` (60/min), per listener, not per client address. Every request, including any new static path, goes through `shared.requests.try_send` to the frame (inbox 64, drain 8 per pass) unless the adapter is changed to answer static files itself before that hand-off, as it already answers 429 and 503.
- Pools: a connection starts in the unauthenticated pool (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `:567`) and moves to the paired pool (12) only on a reply with `authenticated: true` (`:835`). The accept loop closes a fifth stranger at once (accept thread in `bind`, `:660`-ish). A static page reply would be `authenticated: false` (nothing paired about it), so a browser's page, CSS and JS loads, each possibly on parallel TLS connections, all sit in the 4-slot pool.
- Subscriber (`:878`): WebSocket fed from a queue of 256; a revoked device's queue is dropped (`dispatch_inner`, `src/app.rs:486`) and the socket closes.
- `make_identity` (`:95`): `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())` means **no subject alternative names**, CN `Switchboard <server_id>`, key P-256, not_after year 4096. A browser sees a no-SAN, self-signed certificate on an IP-literal host.
- `local_address()` `:962` returns one IPv4 the system routes outward on, or `None`. No hostname, no `.local` name, no IPv6.

### The frame: `src/app.rs`
- `serve_remote` `:3017`. The first line is the allowlist's front door: `request.path.strip_prefix("/api/v1/")`, else a 404 `not_found` (`:3023`). `GET /` today is a 404. `info` and `pair` are served before `authenticate`; everything else needs the bearer.
- `authenticate` `:3127` reads `request.bearer` only. A cookie path means a second source of the token here, and the same function runs `DeviceSeen`.
- `remote_info` `:3568` (what `/info` says: server_id, server_name, protocol, capabilities, `spki_sha256`, version, limits, `pairing_open`). `remote_pair` `:3606` (checks window, then `spki_sha256` equals the host's own key, then code; makes the token; reply `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}`; `device_name` from body, default "Device"). The token travels in the JSON body, so a cookie needs a `Set-Cookie` on this one reply (decision 2).
- `remote_subscribe` `:2723` (requires `request.upgrade`, sends `hello`, registers `Subscriber{device}`); `?scope=all` includes Dispatch workers, plain does not (`hide_workers` `:2687`).
- `bind_remote` `:2936`: `0.0.0.0` when `identity.listen.lan`, else `127.0.0.1` (`:2963`). Bonjour advertises only on LAN.
- The 401 path: `refuse` `:3754` logs method, path and code only; the query is not logged (the path has the query stripped). So the code in `?code=` does not reach the log through `refuse`. [tree] a read of every `log::` that prints a request (none found for the query) would confirm.

### The pairing window UI: `src/ui/remote.rs`
- `pairing` `:141`. The QR payload is built at `:160` as JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses: ["ip:port"]}`, rendered by `qr_texture` (`:172`), and the same string is what "Copy invite" (`:201`) copies. Text beside the QR: spaced code, short key (`short_hash`), address, scope. `window.scope` is chosen in the dialog (radio at the not-open branch) before the window opens; the browser inherits it through `new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs`, `PairedDevice.scope = pairing.scope`).
- The address is `local_address()` + `cx.remote_port` (`src/ui/mod.rs:401, 420`), i.e. a bare IPv4 and the bound port. If `local_address()` is `None` the payload's `addresses` is empty, and a URL has nothing to be a URL of.

## 3. Findings that bear on the decisions

1. **What a self-signed click-through buys is narrower than the issue's framing, and the `key` check has nothing to compare against in the browser.** Page JS cannot read the TLS certificate or its SPKI. The only "key presented by `/info`" available to the page is the `spki_sha256` field of the `/info` JSON, which is whatever the answering server writes. A page served by the impostor serves its own page and its own `/info`. So the URL's `key` guards against reaching the wrong genuine Switchboard by address (a reused DHCP address, two Macs), not against an attacker. On the host side, `remote_pair` (`:3606`) already refuses a `/pair` whose body key is not the host's own, and the page would put the URL's key in that body: against a genuine host that is the only meaningful check; against an impostor the impostor decides. That is the same as the issue's own statement; the notes add that the comparison is page-side and unenforceable from the host's point of view.
2. **Cookies are not port-scoped.** A cookie set by `https://192.168.1.5:43187` is sent to every other port on that host, and a `__Host-` prefix constrains Domain/Path/Secure but not port. Two Switchboard instances on one machine (the dev aid `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, and tests use it) would share a cookie name unless it carries the server id. `SameSite=Strict` is about site, not origin, so another page on a different port of the same IP is same-site: CSRF on `POST /send` and cross-site-WebSocket-hijack protections need an explicit check (Origin or Host, or a custom request header), none of which exists, because the port has only ever had bearer headers, which a cross-origin page cannot attach. Moving to ambient credentials (a cookie) removes that property for the whole `/api/v1` surface, including the native clients' routes: the cookie is accepted at the same endpoints. This is the largest security consequence of decision 2 and should be named in the plan.
3. **The unauthenticated pool is 4 and a browser's page load is bursty.** HTML, CSS, JS, favicon, `/info`, each possibly on its own TLS connection (browsers open up to ~6 per host), all unauthenticated until a reply with `authenticated: true`. A page load by a stranger-or-owner can occupy the pool, and the pool does not distinguish a browser from a flood. Static replies are also not rate-limited. If the page is served on the frame, it competes with the 8-per-pass drain and the 64 inbox; if served on the connection thread, that skips the frame (and the rule "handlers are thin; no logic in the adapter") but needs a pool decision. A paired browser also holds a paired slot per WebSocket for as long as the tab lives, out of 12 shared with the headset and the CLI.
4. **The pairing code lands in the host's request line.** A URL `GET /?code=...` is read by `read_request` into `RemoteRequest.query` (`:496-505`), so the code crosses the TLS connection and sits in the frame's memory like any query. It is not logged by `refuse` (path only). Also: the browser's history entry exists until `replaceState` runs, a `Referer` carries the URL to any subresource that is not same-origin (there should be none under the CSP the issue asks for), and some browsers sync history or open links from a camera app in a different process before the page script runs. A fragment (`#code=`) never reaches the host or a Referer and `replaceState` still works on it; the issue chose the query string. Whether that is deliberate is a question, not a finding.
5. **The code is single use, the URL is a bearer of it.** Anyone who can see the QR for the five-minute window (a screen share, a photo of the dialog) has the code; the key in the QR does not authenticate the person, as today with the JSON QR. No change from the native flow, but the URL is now also in the phone's camera/Messages/clipboard apps. Equivalent to "Copy invite".
6. **Cert has no SAN.** Even with the click-through, some browsers apply extra rules to certificates they treat as untrusted (HSTS-like blocks, no "Proceed" on some versions for no-SAN, ATS-like policies on iOS WebKit for `WebSocket`/`fetch`). Whether a no-SAN, IP-literal, self-signed P-256 certificate can be click-through-accepted on iOS Safari and Android Chrome, and whether that acceptance extends to `wss://` and to `fetch` is what decides option A (click-through) versus option B (host offers its certificate). Not checked.
7. **The spec's sentences to amend** (the plan is told to amend the spec and the status section): `docs/remote-client.md` §4.1 (bounds: "a TLS handshake..."; the pools; add the page's place in them), §4.3 (add the static paths, which are outside the `/api/v1` allowlist and not in the table; "Everything else on the wire is refused before translation" holds for `/api/v1` only), §5 (line 306 "Require pairing before anything but /info and /pair"; line 309 the QR payload JSON, "scans or types both"; line 312 "It is sent only as a bearer header ... never in a URL", which a cookie contradicts; line 313 "The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain"; line 317 "The client verifies the pin on every connection" which a browser cannot), and the design.md sections "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (A1 sentence on "everything else is refused by name", "the QR carrying the server id, key hash, code and address") and "Known gaps". README (Layout row for `web/`, `src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/ui/remote.rs`, `tests/remote.rs`; dev aids; the `pbpaste` pairing line at ~276), CHANGELOG Unreleased line, and the dialog's text.
8. **Static assets and the layering rule.** The page files are data embedded with `include_str!` (no precedent for text assets in `src`, only `include_bytes!` for fonts and the icon in `src/main.rs:167`, `src/ui/theme.rs:203`). A `web/` directory at the repo root would also need `Cargo.toml` `include`/`exclude` and the bundle script checks (`scripts/bundle.sh`) [tree] not read. CLAUDE.md: `src/core` is deterministic and `src/ui` only draws; the page is neither, it is adapter data. Where the path table lives (adapter or `app.rs`) is a design call; `serve_remote` is where the allowlist lives today.
9. **Hard rules touched.** No keystroke injection: not relevant to the page's own JS. Never write into a project's `.claude/`/`.switchboard/`: not touched. Secret values: the page shows redacted text only; the page's CSP and storage choice are what keep a token out of script reach. No client names anywhere that reaches GitHub: nothing in this issue needs one.
